Stage 3 · Language

Comparing, and saying yes or no

How to put two things side by side, and how to turn something down politely.

Read these four lines from three conversations.
  • The statistics look much higher than I’d expect.
  • That sounds much more interesting.
  • I wouldn’t recommend that if you have to work the next day.
  • It was nothing like as good as I expected it to be.
Which one is the strongest way of saying something was bad?
A recommendation is a comparison with a verdict attached.

Saying It’s good gives your listener almost nothing to act on. What makes a recommendation useful is a scale, a comparison and a reason: It’s nowhere near as good as the original, but it’s worth seeing for the soundtrack. This lesson supplies the two language systems that make that kind of sentence possible.

The first is graded comparison. English does not treat all differences as equal, and it has separate expressions for a small gap and a large one. Slightly better, a bit slower, far more entertaining, nowhere near as good as and by far the best are five different claims, and a listener will take them literally. Learning to place a modifier in front of your comparative is what turns a vague impression into information.

The second system is extreme adjectives. Words like terrific, dreadful, stunning, exhausted, freezing, tiny already contain the idea of ‘very’ inside them. Because of that they are ungradable: you cannot say very dreadful or quite freezing, and they resist comparatives too. They take a different family of intensifiers — absolutely, completely, totally, utterly, and the flexible really.

Mixing the two families is one of the most audible errors at this level. Very good is correct; very terrific is not. The practical fix is to keep two mental word banks and never take a word from one bank with an intensifier from the other. That single habit removes most of the problem.

Before you look at the table: the tables below give the comparative and superlative forms first, then the modifiers, then the extreme-adjective pairs. Pay particular attention to the last table — those words behave differently from everything above them.
Comparing two things
What you want to sayThe patternExample
A is bettermore … than / -er thanThe second one is more original than the first.
A is much bettermuch / far / a lot + comparativeThat sounds much more interesting.
A is slightly bettera bit / slightly + comparativeIt’s slightly longer than the original.
They are the sameas … asIt’s as good as everyone says.
A is far worsenothing like as … asIt was nothing like as good as I expected.
A is the topthe + superlativeIt’s the most entertaining game I’ve ever played.
Recommending, and turning something down
 WarmCareful
YesIt’s definitely worth seeing. · I’d highly recommend it.It’s worth a look if you like that sort of thing.
NoI wouldn’t recommend it. · It’s really not worth seeing.I’m pretty sure you wouldn’t like it. · It’s not really my sort of thing.
Suggesting insteadWhy don’t we…? · We could…If you’re really sure, there’s… on the other channel.

Never use two comparatives at once. Not more better, not more easier. One -er or one more, never both.

Than after a comparative, as after as. Better than, as good as — never as good than.

Softening a no. In English, a flat It’s bad sounds harsh. I wouldn’t recommend it and It’s not really my sort of thing say the same thing without insulting the person who suggested it.

And the adverb rule recycled from the vocabulary stage: incredibly goes with normal adjectives, absolutely with extreme ones. Not very exhausted, but absolutely exhausted.

Full grammar reference — comparing and recommending — and extreme adjectives

What it is

Two linked strands. The first is the comparison language used to place one thing against another: not nearly as … as, nowhere near as good as, far better than. The second is extreme adjectives — words such as terrific, dreadful, stunning, exhausted — which already contain the idea of ‘very’ and therefore take a different set of intensifiers.

What it means, and what it does

Recommending is comparing with a verdict attached. It’s good tells your listener very little; It’s nowhere near as good as the original, but it’s worth seeing for the soundtrack gives them a scale, a comparison and a reason to act. Extreme adjectives then let you deliver the verdict in one word instead of three — which is why reviews are full of them.

When and why we use it

Saying It’s good gives your listener almost nothing to act on. What makes a recommendation useful is a scale, a comparison and a reason: It’s nowhere near as good as the original, but it’s worth seeing for the soundtrack. This lesson supplies the two language systems that make that kind of sentence possible.

The first is graded comparison. English does not treat all differences as equal, and it has separate expressions for a small gap and a large one. Slightly better, a bit slower, far more entertaining, nowhere near as good as and by far the best are five different claims, and a listener will take them literally. Learning to place a modifier in front of your comparative is what turns a vague impression into information.

The second system is extreme adjectives. Words like terrific, dreadful, stunning, exhausted, freezing, tiny already contain the idea of ‘very’ inside them. Because of that they are ungradable: you cannot say very dreadful or quite freezing, and they resist comparatives too. They take a different family of intensifiers — absolutely, completely, totally, utterly, and the flexible really.

Mixing the two families is one of the most audible errors at this level. Very good is correct; very terrific is not. The practical fix is to keep two mental word banks and never take a word from one bank with an intensifier from the other. That single habit removes most of the problem.

Typical situations

You need this language for reviewing films, games, restaurants and products, for recommending or warning somebody off, and for any conversation where you compare two things and say which you prefer.

  • Saying two things are equal — as … as.The remake is as long as the original.
  • Saying one is clearly worse — not nearly as … as, nowhere near as … as.It’s nowhere near as good as I expected.
  • Measuring the size of a difference — far, much, a lot (big) · slightly, a bit (small) + comparative.The soundtrack is far better than the script.
  • Naming the best or worst — superlative + by far, easily.Freeman’s performance is by far the best thing in it.
  • Recommending — I’d definitely recommend…, It’s a must-see, It’s worth…I’d definitely recommend seeing it on a big screen.
  • Advising against — Don’t bother with…, I wouldn’t bother…Don’t bother with the sequel.
  • Delivering a strong verdict — an extreme adjective, with no very.The special effects are absolutely stunning.

How it differs from similar structures

not as good as (neutral, a bit worse) · not nearly as good as (much worse) · nowhere near as good as (much worse, informal and emphatic). The three are not interchangeable in strength.
good takes very; terrific takes absolutely. Grading words and extreme words each have their own intensifiers, and mixing them is one of the most audible B1 errors.

How to build it

Equality: as + adjective + as
Inequality: not as / not nearly as / nowhere near as + adjective + as
Modified comparative: far / much / a lot / slightly / a bit + comparative + than
Extreme adjective: absolutely / really / totally + extreme adjective  (never very)
Comparative — short adjectives+ -er: long → longer, silly → sillier
Comparative — long adjectivesmore + adjective: more entertaining, more predictable
Superlativethe + -est / the most + adjective: the silliest, the most disturbing
Irregulargood → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further
Negative comparisonIt isn’t as good as the book. · It’s not nearly as good.
QuestionWhich is better, the book or the film?
Extreme adjectives — the pairsgood → terrific / brilliant · bad → dreadful / awful · big → huge · small → tiny · tired → exhausted · cold → freezing · surprising → astonishing
Intensifiers that fit extremesabsolutely, completely, totally, utterly, really — but not very.

Spelling and word order

  • One-syllable adjective ending in one vowel + one consonant doubles it: big → bigger, sad → saddest.
  • Consonant + y becomes -ier / -iest: silly → sillier → the silliest.
  • Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y, -er, -ow, -le usually take -er; most other two-syllable and all longer adjectives take more.
  • Fun is an exception in careful English: prefer more fun to funner.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • than is weak in speech, reduced to /ðən/, and often sounds like then. Do not confuse them in writing.
  • The stress in a comparison falls on the adjective, not on as: nowhere near as GOOD as.
  • Extreme adjectives usually carry a wide falling pitch, which is part of what makes them sound emphatic: ab-so-LUTE-ly DREAD-ful.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Never use very with an extreme adjective. Very exhausted, very freezing and very brilliant are all wrong; the word already carries the extreme. Use absolutely or really instead.
  • Extreme adjectives are ungradable: they also resist comparatives and superlatives. More exhausted is possible in casual speech but the most freezing is not.
  • Really is the flexible one: it works with both normal and extreme adjectives (really good, really terrific).
  • Double comparatives are an error: more better, more easier. Choose -er or more, never both.
  • The superlative takes the, even after a possessive-free noun: the best performance, not best performance.
  • Worth is followed by -ing: worth seeing, not worth to see.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • The sequel is very dreadful. → The sequel is absolutely dreadful.Dreadful is extreme, so it cannot take very.
  • It’s more better than the original. → It’s much better than the original.Never combine more with an -er form.
  • It’s nowhere near as good than the book. → It’s nowhere near as good as the book.The as … as structure takes as, not than.
  • Freeman gives best performance in the film. → Freeman gives the best performance in the film.Superlatives take the.
  • It’s worth to see on a big screen. → It’s worth seeing on a big screen.Worth is followed by -ing.
  • I recommend you to see it. → I’d recommend seeing it. / I recommend that you see it.Recommend does not take somebody to do in standard English.

More examples in context

  • equalityThe remake is just as long as the original, and half as interesting.
  • clear inferiorityIt’s nowhere near as frightening as people said.
  • small differenceThe soundtrack is slightly better than I remembered.
  • large differenceThe special effects are far more impressive than the plot.
  • superlativeIt’s by far the most entertaining game I’ve ever played.
  • extreme adjectiveThe last twenty minutes are absolutely stunning.
  • extreme adjectiveThe dialogue is utterly dreadful in places.
  • recommendingI’d definitely recommend it — although not if you want something short.
  • must-seeHonestly, it’s a must-see.
  • advising againstDon’t bother with the first half hour; it’s very slow.

A tip for remembering it

Keep two separate word banks in your head. Bank A holds normal adjectives and their intensifiers: very good, quite silly, a bit slow. Bank B holds extreme adjectives and theirs: absolutely terrific, completely dreadful, really exhausted. Never take a word from one bank and an intensifier from the other.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. As … as for equality; not nearly / nowhere near as … as for a big gap.
  2. Measure a difference with far, much, a lot (big) or slightly, a bit (small) before the comparative.
  3. Never combine more with an -er ending; superlatives always take the.
  4. Extreme adjectives already mean ‘very’ — use absolutely, completely, really, never very.
  5. Worth and recommend are followed by -ing.
  6. A recommendation works best as comparison + verdict + reason.

Stage 5 · Main input

A review that helps somebody decide

Read it as a writer. You are going to write one like it.

Before you read: what do you actually want from a review?

Choose one. The model does two of these, and deliberately avoids one.

The Shawshank Redemption — still worth two hours

Some films get better the second time you watch them. This is one of them.

Based on a novel by Stephen King and released in 1994, it tells the story of a banker who is falsely sent to prison for killing his wife. He soon makes friends with another prisoner, and the two of them spend the next twenty years finding small ways to stay human inside a place designed to prevent exactly that.

The cast is excellent. Morgan Freeman’s performance is the most moving thing in the film, and Thomas Newman’s soundtrack creates an atmosphere you remember long afterwards. It is not perfect: the first half hour is incredibly slow, and one or two of the prison scenes are quite violent. But the last twenty minutes are absolutely brilliant, and I am not going to say why.

Compared with most prison dramas, it is far less interested in escape and far more interested in friendship. It is nothing like as depressing as it sounds. The film is sad in places, but essentially it is a positive story.

Despite failing at the box office when it was originally released, it has since become a modern classic. On balance, I would highly recommend it — although not if you are looking for something short.

What the model does, in five moves
  • Opens with a claim, not with the plot.
  • Gives the facts in one paragraph — and stops before the ending.
  • Says what is good and what is not. A review with no criticism is not believed.
  • Compares it with something the reader knows. That is what tells them whether they will like it.
  • Ends with a verdict and a condition: I’d recommend it — unless…
